extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent attorneys/agents, and practitioners evaluating pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) bars (public use or on-sale) invalidate patentability — tests, evidence, and policy considerations with case examples. Applies to examiner rejections and practitioner counseling for pre-AIA filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between public use and on-sale bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) “contains several distinct bars to patentability, each of which relates to activity or disclosure more than one year prior to the date of the application. Two of these - the ‘public use’ and the ‘on sale’ objections - are sometimes considered together although it is quite clear that either may apply when the other does not.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'public use' and 'on sale' as separate statutory bars that can independently trigger invalidity; analyze facts for each because similar activity may implicate one but not the other (examples and cases cited: Dart Indus.; Hobbs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for 'public use' (Pfaff-related context)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public use bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) arises where the invention is in public use before the critical date and is ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the purported use (1) was accessible to the public; or (2) was commercially exploited. Consider evidence relevant to experimentation, nature of activity in public, public access to the use, confidentiality obligations on observers, and commercial exploitation (Invitrogen Corp. v. Biocrest). See also MPEP § 2133.03(c) for the 'ready for patenting' prong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public knowledge is not necessarily public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere knowledge of the invention by the public does not warrant rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b). 102(b) bars public use or sale, not public knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate publications or public awareness alone with a public-use bar; distinguish 102(a) (publications) from 102(b) (use/sale). (Case: TP Labs. v. Professional Positioners.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial versus noncommercial use and impact of secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret or confidential use alone is not necessarily sufficient to create a public use bar; commercial exploitation combined with secrecy can. Non-commercial activity may be treated differently than commercial activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether use was commercial exploitation (more likely to be public use) versus non-commercial/internal use (less likely). Consider MPEP §§ 2133.03(c) and 2133.03(e) and cited cases (Invitrogen; examples where internal secret use did not create a bar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsecret (visible) use is not ipso facto public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-secret uses of a device prior to the critical date are not themselves dispositive of a public use determination; nonsecret does not automatically equal public use, nor is secret use automatically not public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine totality of circumstances (control, restrictions, publicity, commercial exploitation). (Case: TP Labs.; Moleculon cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Display within larger article can be public use
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor or someone connected with the inventor puts the invention on display or sells it as part of a larger machine or article accessible to the public and used naturally/intendedly, that is public use even if inner workings are hidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess accessibility to visitors and whether the public could observe/use the invention's relevant features (In re Blaisdell; Ex parte Kuklo; Hall v. Macneale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private use for inventor's enjoyment is not public use
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor’s private use of the invention, restricted to locations with a reasonable expectation of privacy and for personal enjoyment, is not a public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for retention of control and limitation to close acquaintances in private settings (Moleculon Research Corp. v. CBS example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or absence of confidentiality agreement not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence or absence of a confidentiality agreement is not dispositive of public use, but is one factor in assessing the totality of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider confidentiality agreements among other factors (nature of activity, public access, policies underlying bars). Courts may remand where examiner focused solely on absence of agreement (Bernhardt v. Collezione Europa example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use when inventor allows another to use without restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Public use’ occurs when the inventor allows another person to use the invention without limitation, restriction or obligation of secrecy to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the inventor retained control or imposed obligations; absent such control, use by another can be a public-use bar (In re Smith; Ex parte C; Egbert v. Lippmann).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by independent third parties can be public use if it 'informs' the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Use by someone unconnected to the inventor may be public use if it sufficiently informs the public of the invention or a competitor could reasonably ascertain the invention (including by inspection/analysis of sold/displayed products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether details are ascertainable from products, whether many employees had access without secrecy, or affirmative steps were taken to educate employees; if user maintained trade secrecy and invention not ascertainable, it may not be public use (Gillman; Dunlop; W.L. Gore & Assocs.; Manville Sales Corp.; Chemithon/Proctor & Gamble example).

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar Pfaff two-prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: The on-sale bar is triggered if, more than one year before the effective filing date, (1) the invention was the subject of a commercial offer for sale not primarily for experimental purposes, and (2) the invention was ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Pfaff v. Wells Elecs. to determine both commercial offer (look to traditional contract law/UCC) and readiness for patenting (see entry on 'ready for patenting').

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'sale' for on-sale bar (UCC §2-106 guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale is a contract where seller passes rights of property to buyer for a price. To be 'on sale', a product must be subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale bearing hallmarks of a sale pursuant to UCC §2-106.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider passage of title as an indicator; contract law principles and UCC guide whether communications constitute a commercial offer (Medicines Co. v. Hospira en banc explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional sales and experimental-use inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: A conditional sale may still bar a patent; conditioning on buyer satisfaction does not, without more, prove the sale was for experimental purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the transaction's purpose was experimental or commercial exploitation (Strong v. General Elec. example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonprofit sale can be 'on sale' if commercially exploited
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale need not be for profit to bar a patent; if sale was for commercial exploitation of the invention, it is on sale within the meaning of §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't dismiss non-profit transfers; evaluate commercial exploitation aspects (In re Dybel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single sale or single offer can bar patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a single sale or offer to sell the invention may bar patentability under pre-AIA §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single transaction more than one year before filing can be sufficient (Consolidated Fruit-Jar Co.; Atlantic Thermoplastics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of patent rights is not necessarily sale of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment or sale of rights in the invention/potential patent rights is not a sale of 'the invention' within §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish assignments/licenses that transfer only legal rights from transactions that transfer embodiments or title to the inventive product; licenses that effectively transfer the product (e.g., certain software licenses) may still trigger on-sale (Moleculon; Group One; Elan Corp. discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract manufacturer/service sales generally do not constitute 'sale' of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of manufacturing services by a contract manufacturer to an inventor, where neither title to embodiments nor the right to market passes to the supplier, does not constitute an invalidating sale under §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether title or marketing rights passed; mere commercial benefit to parties is insufficient—product must be commercially marketed (Medicines Co. v. Hospira).

rubrics_metrics.name: Buyer must be independent/uncontrolled for on-sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale or offer for sale must be between separate entities; where parties are related, whether a bar exists depends on whether seller controls buyer so invention remains out of public hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess degree of control (e.g., parent/subsidiary with unfettered buyer management may still create a bar) (In re Caveney; Ferag AG v. Quipp example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offers for sale require material terms and ability to form binding contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Only an offer that rises to level of a commercial offer for sale—one the other party could make into a binding contract by simple acceptance—constitutes an offer for sale under §102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for material terms (price, quantity, delivery, specifications); communications lacking such terms may not be 'offers' (Group One; Elan Corp. case where letter lacked material terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejected or unreceived offers and lack of delivery can still create on-sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere offer to sell is sufficient to bar a patent; even a rejected or unreceived offer may create an on-sale bar. Delivery or consummation of sale is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine timing of offer and whether it constituted a commercial offer regardless of acceptance or delivery (In re Theis; UMC Elecs.; Buildex; Weatherchem examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goods need not be on hand; readiness and immediacy considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Seller need not have goods 'on hand' when offer made; the date of the offer is the effective date of 'on sale' activity, but the invention must be 'ready for patenting' before the critical date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess completeness/readiness (see Pfaff 'ready for patenting' prong). If inventor was not close to completion, offer may not trigger bar (Micro Chemical example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence of sale/offer controls over uncommunicated intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence such as descriptions in contracts, correspondence, drawings, order confirmations, etc., controls over an uncommunicated intent by seller to deliver the inventive product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require documentary objective proof that the product offered/sold embodied the claimed invention; purchaser's reasonable beliefs also relevant (Ferag; RCA Corp. v. Data Gen.; Envirotech examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales/offers by independent third parties can bar patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale or offer for sale by an independent third party more than one year before filing will bar applicant from obtaining a patent, except where a patented method's secret remains secret after sale of an unpatented product by another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat third-party commercial sales similarly to inventor sales for bar analysis unless trade secrecy preserved and invention not ascertainable (In re Caveney).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-prior-art publications may serve as evidence of sale before critical date
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts or publications that identify a product vendor and provide buyer-useful info (release or installation dates, contact, price, documentation) before applicant's critical date may provide sufficient evidence of prior sale for a 102(b) or 103 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contemporaneous product announcements, abstracts, release/installation dates as objective evidence of commercial availability (In re Epstein example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ready for patenting — reduction to practice or enabling description
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Pfaff, 'ready for patenting' may be satisfied either by reduction to practice before the critical date or by prior drawings/descriptions sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate (a) whether invention was actually reduced to practice (testing under working conditions showing practical utility), or (b) whether drawings/specifications before critical date contained each claim element and enabled practice (Pfaff; Weatherchem; Vanmoor; Abbott Labs. examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent possession of claim limitations in offered product
rubrics_metrics.description: If a product offered for sale inherently possesses each limitation of the claims, the invention is on sale even if parties did not recognize the claimed characteristics at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intrinsic characteristics of sold product; subjective qualities do not avoid the on-sale bar (Abbott Laboratories; STX LLC v. Brine examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice requires demonstration of practical utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual reduction to practice in on-sale contexts usually requires testing under actual working conditions demonstrating practical utility beyond probability of failure, unless invention is so simple that operativeness is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for testing/demonstration evidence showing operability; mere prototypes or incomplete development may not suffice (Field v. Knowles; Steinberg v. Seitz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention need not be ready for commercial marketing to trigger bar
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention need not be ready for satisfactory commercial marketing for sale to bar a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate readiness for patenting with readiness for marketability; limited commercial readiness does not preclude an on-sale bar (Atlantic Thermoplastics Co. v. Faytex).
